overall_feedback: This is an inventive experiment. Using a graphene p-n junction to build a Mach-Zehnder interferometer with a probe integer edge of known spin is a clean idea for resolving the spin of fractional edge channels. The integer-regime calibration (-2,1), (-2,2), (-1,1), together with the presence or absence of interference at (-1,2/3) and (-2,2/3) on either side of the B of about 9.5 T transition, convincingly separates a spin-polarized interface channel at high field from one that couples to both spin species at low field. I checked the theory closely and found it internally consistent: the charge/spin decomposition of the K = [[1,2],[2,1]] electron operators, the velocities in Eq. (S15), the saddle point S* in Notes 5 and 6, the closed form C = 8 pi log 2 - 4 i pi^2 (from Beta-function integrals), the Peierls phase, and the arithmetic giving Delta t from B_nm all hold up. The weaknesses are in the quantitative link between theory and data, and in how far the claims go. (i) The extracted time delays (1.67 to 7.31 ps) put the experiment well outside the high-temperature regime kBT >> hbar/Delta t used to derive Eqs. (3)-(5): the conditions require several kelvin. (ii) The three decay rates fix the three unknowns exactly, with no uncertainties and no overdetermination, so the fit cannot test the model. (iii) The implied neutral-mode velocity (above 3e5 m/s) is in tension with the paper's own framing. (iv) The data show an unpolarized, interacting two-component edge with frequency mixing. They do not separately establish SU(2) spin-singlet order or the specific spin-swap mechanism, and the supplement itself shows that the f_nm survive SU(2) breaking. The assignment of f10 and f01 to spin species also rests on a 6% area difference, and a stray annotation in Supplementary Note 7 makes the labeling uncertain. Most of these issues can be fixed by fitting the full finite-temperature expressions, reporting uncertainties, using the parameter-free amplitude ratio the theory predicts, and toning down the claims about singlet order.

comments.title: Extracted time delays violate the high-temperature condition used to derive Eqs. (3)-(5)
comments.quote: In the high-temperature regime kB T ≫ ℏ/∆t↑ , ℏ/∆ts ,
comments.explanation: Eqs. (3)-(5) are asymptotic forms valid only for kBT >> hbar/Delta t, and the Delta t values are then extracted by fitting these forms to data. My first thought was that this condition might be loose in practice because the exponent carries a factor pi. So I checked against the authors' own noninteracting benchmark, Eq. (S2), where Vis is proportional to x/sinh x with x = pi kB T Delta t/hbar. Even with that factor the fitted values are not self-consistent. With hbar/kB = 7.64 ps K: hbar/(kB Delta t_down) = 4.6 K for Delta t_down = 1.67 ps, hbar/(kB Delta t_s) = 3.5 K, and hbar/(kB Delta t_up) = 1.0 K. The f11 condition kBT >> hbar/(l/vNc) needs T >> 3.5 K, because l/vNc < Delta t_s = 2.18 ps. The visibilities are normalized at 100 mK and the coherent-interference data presumably extend only to around 1 K. For B01 = 2.76 ps the argument pi kB T B/hbar is about 1.1 at 1 K. In the range x of roughly 0.2 to 1, the local log-slope of x/sinh x is coth x - 1/x, about 0.16 to 0.31 of its asymptotic value, and it reaches only 0.67 at x = 3. A linear fit of log Vis over such a window therefore underestimates the asymptotic decay constant by a large and parameter-dependent factor, and the mapping of B_nm onto Eq. (S14) breaks down. Excluding the three lowest-temperature points acknowledges a low-T deviation but does not address this crossover. The specific numbers, and the conclusions drawn from them (velocity ordering, the spin mode being faster than the spin-up electrons), are not reliable as stated.
comments.suggested_fix: Fit the measured visibilities with the full finite-temperature integrals, Eq. (S3) and Eq. (S10), evaluated numerically over the measured temperature window (the authors already integrate Eq. (S10) numerically to check Eq. (S13)). Also state the temperature range and the values of pi kB T Delta t/hbar reached. If these stay below about 2, report the fitted B_nm as lower bounds on the asymptotic delays.

comments.title: Three decay rates determine three unknowns exactly, so the fit is not a test of the model and has no stated uncertainty
comments.quote: From the fitting, we estimate B10 = 8.41 ps, B01 = 2.76 ps, B11 = 8.98 ps.
comments.explanation: I verified the inversion: Delta t_s = B10 + B01 - B11 = 2.19 ps, Delta t_up = 7.31 ps and Delta t_down = 1.67 ps, all consistent. However, Eq. (S14) is three linear equations in three unknowns, so almost any three measured decay rates produce a solution. The only nontrivial outcome is positivity, which is weak evidence. No fit uncertainties are given. Because Delta t_s is a difference of three numbers of order 3 to 9 ps, a 10% error on B11 (about 0.9 ps) alone shifts Delta t_s by about 40%. The supplement says the extraction is 'rendered inconclusive', yet the Methods present the values without that caveat and call them consistent with typical velocities. The f02 component is measured (Fig. 3e), but its conductance is explicitly not derived. Deriving it is exactly what would make the system overdetermined and the comparison a genuine test.
comments.suggested_fix: Report fit uncertainties on B10, B01 and B11 and propagate them to Delta t_up, Delta t_down and Delta t_s. Copy the 'inconclusive' caveat from Supplementary Note 7 into the Methods. Derive the leading exponent for the (0,2) term and compare it with the measured f02 decay as an independent check.

comments.title: Velocities implied by the extracted delays are in tension with the stated consistency and with the model
comments.quote: The extracted time delays are on the picosecond scale, as expected from the typical edge velocity v ∼ 1 × 105 m/s
comments.explanation: The delays being 'picosecond scale' seemed like a reasonable sanity check until I worked out the bounds they imply directly. Since Delta t_s = l/vNs + l/vNc = 2.18 ps with l = 700 nm, both vNs and vNc must exceed l/Delta t_s, about 3.2e5 m/s. Then l/vP_up = 7.31 ps + l/vNc lies between 7.31 and 9.49 ps, so vP_up is about 0.74e5 to 0.96e5 m/s. Similarly vP_down exceeds 1.8e5 m/s, more than twice vP_up, even though both are integer channels in the same p region. In the model's own SU(2) parametrization, vs = v - v_updown and vc = (v + v_updown)/3, so the bare velocity v = (vs + 3 vc)/2 must exceed about 6.4e5 m/s. The neutral spin mode, which repulsion slows in this model, would then be more than three times faster than the integer channels. Neutral modes in FQH edges are usually reported as slower than charge modes. These figures follow from the paper's numbers, so describing them as 'as expected' understates a real tension, which may be a symptom of the regime problem raised above.
comments.suggested_fix: Replace the consistency sentence with the explicit bounds implied by Eq. (S14): vNs, vNc > 3.2e5 m/s, vP_up of about (0.74-0.96)e5 m/s, and vP_down > 1.8e5 m/s. Discuss them against reported neutral-mode and integer-edge velocities in graphene.

comments.title: Normalization by measured dI00/dV and the weak-tunneling assumption affect the individual Delta t values
comments.quote: The power-law prefactor is not quantitatively
comments.explanation: The theory is perturbative in the beam-splitter tunneling and predicts dI00/dV proportional to T and dInm/dV proportional to T^(n+m). I checked that the prediction for I00 is right: tunneling from an integer electron (dimension 1/2) into the 2/3 electron (dimension 1) gives G proportional to T^1. The authors then report that the power law is not reproduced, and divide by the measured (dI00/dV)^(n+m) to define Vis_nm. Suppose the measured dI00/dV carries extra temperature dependence, say T exp(-kappa pi kB T/hbar). Then B10 and B01 both shift by kappa and B11 by 2 kappa. Delta t_s = B10 + B01 - B11 is unchanged, but Delta t_up and Delta t_down shift by a common kappa. The individual spin-resolved delays therefore depend on an unmodeled normalization. The failure of the power law also hints that the beam splitters are not in the weak-tunneling regime where Eqs. (3)-(5) apply: Fig. 2b shows sizable raw transmission, and a fourth-order term (f11) is clearly visible. Separately, the Methods say Eqs. (3)-(5) are compared with 'the experimental data in Fig. 3e', but Fig. 3e shows visibilities normalized at 100 mK, while the fit uses the differently defined Vis_nm.
comments.suggested_fix: Show the measured T dependence of dI00/dV and the beam-splitter transmissions T1, T2 in the low-field regime. As a cross-check, fit the raw |dInm/dV| with a free power-law prefactor T^p times exp(-B pi kB T/hbar). Change the Methods sentence to say the fit uses Vis_nm as defined in Supplementary Note 7.

comments.title: Assignment of f10 and f01 to spin-up and spin-down rests on a 6% area difference
comments.quote: The different AB areas identify f10 and f01 with
comments.explanation: The ordering is plausible: the spin-up channel is the outermost hole channel of the p region (the only one at nu_P = -1), so it should sit closer to the n-region channel and enclose a smaller area, and 0.082 < 0.087 um^2 agrees. But the two areas correspond to arm separations of about 117 and 124 nm, a 7 nm difference. In the same low-field regime at (-1,2/3) (Fig. 3a), the spin-up loop has area 0.121 um^2 (about 173 nm). That is about 50% larger than f10. The area of a given spin's loop therefore moves by far more between gate configurations than the f10-f01 difference used for the assignment. The Vleft frequencies (72.8 vs 21.2 V^-1) differ much more, but they are not used. The assignment matters for interpretation: Eq. (S14) is symmetric under relabeling, but the claims that Delta t_up is much larger than Delta t_down and that the spin mode is faster than the spin-up electrons depend on which peak is which.
comments.suggested_fix: Base the assignment on an independent control. For example, follow the single (-1,2/3) spin-up peak continuously as nu_P is tuned to -2 along the same gate axis, or measure Fig. 3a against Vleft so its lever arm can be compared with 72.8 and 21.2 V^-1. Also quote the FFT peak width along the B axis to show that the 0.005 um^2 separation is resolved.

comments.title: Stray annotation suggests the 10/01 labels may have been swapped in the decay analysis
comments.explanation: This fragment appears in Supplementary Note 7 beneath Fig. S3 with no context. It looks like a leftover note saying that the (1,0) and (0,1) labels were interchanged for the figure or the fit. Given the fragile spin assignment discussed above, a reader cannot tell whether B10 = 8.41 ps refers to the (0.082 um^2, 72.8 V^-1) peak that the main text calls spin-up (red in Fig. 3e), or to the other peak. If the labels are swapped relative to the main text, Delta t_up and Delta t_down swap, and the conclusion about which electrons the spin mode outruns changes.
comments.suggested_fix: Remove the annotation. State explicitly in the Fig. S3 caption which panel corresponds to the (0.082 um^2, 72.8 V^-1) peak and which to the (0.087 um^2, 21.2 V^-1) peak, using the same labels and colors as Fig. 3c,e.

comments.title: Data establish an unpolarized interacting edge; spin-singlet (SU(2)) order specifically is not separately demonstrated
comments.quote: Our results establish edge transport as a probe of spin-singlet topological orders [1, 6, 23],
comments.explanation: The direct spin-resolved result is solid: at low field the interface channel couples to both spin-up and spin-down probes, so it is unpolarized. Going from 'unpolarized' to 'spin-singlet with an SU(2) spin mode' is a further step. The filling description (1,1,1/3,1/3) alone does not distinguish the (112)-type singlet with a counterpropagating neutral mode from, for example, a (330)-like state of two spin-resolved 1/3 Laughlin edges, both downstream. The observables that could discriminate are f11 and the thermal decay rates. Supplementary Note 8, however, shows that the f_nm and the electron-charge AB period survive when SU(2) is broken. Their presence therefore evidences the K = [[1,2],[2,1]] counterpropagating structure, not the SU(2) symmetry. The decay fit is exactly determined (see above) and assumes the SU(2) exponents 3/2 and 1/2, so it cannot confirm them. In graphene there is an added subtlety: the two fractional components must be specified in both spin and valley. If they also differ in valley, a spin rotation does not map one onto the other and SU(2) spin symmetry is not the natural symmetry of the interaction. The title and abstract claims of 'spin-singlet' edges and topological order therefore go beyond what the measurements establish independently.
comments.suggested_fix: Either reword to 'spin-unpolarized nu = 2/3 edge consistent with the spin-singlet (112) structure', or add an explicit comparison showing that a (330)-type edge, or a K = [[1,2],[2,1]] edge with substantial SU(2) breaking, predicts measurably different f_nm content or decay exponents than those observed. Also state the valley indices of the two 1/3 components.

comments.title: f11 shows frequency mixing; the spin-swap two-electron mechanism is inferred from the model, not isolated by the data
comments.quote: In particular, f11 represents interference involving two
comments.explanation: I agree that a sum frequency cannot appear in a noninteracting spin-conserving MZI, so f11 does signal interactions. But any coupling between the two AB loops that share the n-region arm could produce f10 + f01. Capacitive (Coulomb) coupling, which makes the phase of one loop depend on the occupation of the other, is one example; nonlinearity in how delta T is extracted is another, and delta T is never defined. The spin swap is the model's interpretation of a fourth-order perturbative term in a linear-response conductance. It is not a measured two-particle correlation like the noise-based HBT or HOM effects it is contrasted with. The theory does provide a sharper test that goes unused. In Eqs. (3)-(5) the velocity factors and tunneling magnitudes cancel in the ratio |dI11/dV| / (|dI10/dV| |dI01/dV|). That leaves a parameter-free prediction: (2|C|/64 pi^4)(hbar/e^2) exp(pi kB T Delta t_s/hbar), which is about 0.41 (h/e^2) exp(pi kB T Delta t_s/hbar) with |C| = 7938. Comparing the measured amplitudes with this ratio would discriminate the proposed mechanism from generic Coulomb mixing.
comments.suggested_fix: Report the measured amplitude ratio |G11|/(|G10||G01|) and compare it with the parameter-free prediction 0.41 (h/e^2) exp(pi kB T Delta t_s/hbar) that follows from Eqs. (3)-(5). Also define how delta T is obtained from T, so that mixing introduced by processing can be excluded.

comments.title: Comparison of thermal decay with the spin-polarized regime does not isolate spin-charge separation
comments.quote: f01 exhibit enhanced thermal decay and bias-voltage de-
comments.explanation: The spin-polarized reference is a different interferometer at a different field (B of about 11 T). It has a different area (0.148 um^2, arm separation about 210 nm versus about 120 nm) and presumably different channel velocities. For a noninteracting MZI, Eq. (S2) gives decay governed by |l/vNd - l/vP_down|, which can take any value. Faster decay in the low-field regime is therefore expected whenever the velocity mismatch is larger, with or without spin-charge separation. The comparison is suggestive but cannot by itself support the attribution to fractionalization-induced decoherence.
comments.suggested_fix: Add a same-field control: measure the thermal decay of the integer (-2,1) or (-2,2) MZI at B of about 8.4 T to calibrate the p-region channel velocities, and use the result to constrain vP_up and vP_down in Eq. (S14).

comments.title: Location of the saddle point is set by the velocity ordering, not by the chargon's larger scaling dimension
comments.quote: contribution occurs for maximal chargon overlap, as the
comments.explanation: I traced S(t) piecewise. The chargon exponent 3/2 exactly equals the sum of the electron (1) and spinon (1/2) exponents. For vNc > vP_up, S has slope +2 on (-l/vNs, l/vNc) and -1 on (l/vNc, l/vP_up), so the maximum is at t = l/vNc as stated. For vNc < vP_up, however, S is flat on [l/vP_up, l/vNc], and the decay constant becomes B10 = (3/2)(l/vNc - l/vP_up) + (1/2)(l/vP_up + l/vNs). The stated justification is therefore incomplete. It also means that the positive Delta t values obtained by inverting Eq. (S14) are not, by themselves, evidence for the assumed ordering. Under the other ordering B10, B01 and B11 have different forms, and the same measured rates might also admit a solution.
comments.suggested_fix: Replace the justification with: 'For vNc > vP_up the maximum of S(t) is at t = l/vNc; for vNc < vP_up, S(t) is constant on [l/vP_up, l/vNc] and B10 = (3/2)(l/vNc - l/vP_up) + (1/2)(l/vP_up + l/vNs).' Then state whether the measured B_nm also admit a solution under the reversed ordering.

comments.title: Role of the Si back gate is described inconsistently
comments.quote: VSi further fine-tunes the separation between the in-
comments.explanation: The main text says VSi tunes the separation of the interfering channels. Supplementary Note 2 says 'VSi is used on the right side to tune contact resistance'. Since the graphite gates screen the Si gate everywhere except the 70 nm slit and the right contact regions, both roles are possible, but the mechanism matters. Fig. 3a, the key evidence that the low-field fractional channel couples to spin-up electrons, is measured against VSi (11.4 V^-1). It therefore cannot be compared with the Vleft frequencies of the spin-up component in Fig. 3c.
comments.suggested_fix: State that VSi gates the junction through the 70 nm slit, in addition to acting on the right contacts, and give its lever arm on the interface channels; or add the (-1,2/3) data as a function of Vleft so it can be compared directly with f10 = (0.082 um^2, 72.8 V^-1).
